Au rythme malheureux où les féminicides: As femicides multiply at an alarming rate in Quebec, the movement against violence against women is gaining ground in the media. Men are speaking out on the subject more and more, and the phenomenon is stirring up controversy. Some see it as the symptom of a deeper problem. Marina Mathieu, an Afrofeminist activist and communications consultant, takes a critical view of the situation. “Unlike men, women don’t seem to me to have put themselves forward.
Par contre, j’ai vu beaucoup de femmes s: But I’ve seen a lot of women question the fact that it’s men who are carrying the message,” she says. “I don’t understand why they’re given so much space without anyone seeing the problem in that.” She wonders how men can take up so much space without realizing that this space should be shared or distributed.
Kharoll-Ann Souffrant, travailleuse soci: Kharoll-Ann Souffrant, a social worker and doctoral student in social work, focuses on the issue of violence against women in her research and teaching. She believes men have to be part of the solution, because they are also part of the problem. “We can’t talk to women all the time; we also have to include men,” says Souffrant, who nonetheless believes it has to be done in a certain way.
« Il y a une tendance à se positionner e: “There’s a tendency to position yourself outside the problem,” she explains. “When people present themselves as the heroes of the story, and it’s not about them, it creates discomfort.”
Pour Will Prosper, Rito Joseph, Ricardo: For Will Prosper, Rito Joseph, Ricardo Lamour and Thierry Lindor, the instigators of the Parle à tes boys initiative, the death of Rebecca Harrison, who was killed by her partner, was “the last straw.” Since last February, in the wake of<l1> the Camara affair</l1>, the four public figures, who have become friends, have made a habit of having long phone conversations to discuss issues affecting their communities.
C’est ainsi qu’est née la campagne Parle: That is how the Parle à tes boys campaign was born. It invites men to have conversations, to dismantle patriarchy and sexism, and to rethink the way they act. Recently launched, the movement quickly gained momentum. The group sees the direct effects of such a project on the public. The initiative strikes a chord in particular with young men, who open up, confide in them and join the discussion.
« Le réel pouvoir de Parle à tes boys es: “The real power of Parle à tes boys is its ability to infiltrate a toxic masculinity that has existed for too long in our communities,” says Thierry Lindor. Like his colleague Will Prosper, he wonders whether the people he is speaking to would have felt as called out by well-known female figures who speak out. “I’m not saying yes or no,” he answers, honestly. He is instead happy with the result and with the fact that people seem to appreciate that he is using his platform for this purpose.
« La cause n’est pas populaire, surtout: “The cause isn’t popular, especially among men; that happens when you talk about something that makes them individually uncomfortable,” he argues.
Le succès de Parle à tes boys s’est fait: The success of Parle à tes boys was felt everywhere and benefited from significant media visibility. NDP leader Jagmeet Singh wore a campaign T-shirt on his most recent appearance on Tout le monde en parle. “The goal was never to seek attention,” adds Thierry Lindor. “We simply wanted to get together as men and boys. Our hearts were in the right place. It started from there, and it exploded.”
Il estime qu’au moins, cette visibilité: He believes that at least this visibility allows the message to reach men. The situation seems familiar to Alexandrine Beauvais Lamoureux, an international law student. “I hope this tendency to listen more to men on subjects that, concretely, don’t affect them gets called into question,” she says. For the Collège Jean-Eudes alumna, the issue is the hypersexualization of young girls through their uniforms.
L’automne dernier, les garçons de l’écol: Last fall, boys at the high school mobilized to denounce sexist bias by wearing skirts. The initiative caused a stir at the school and was reported in the media. Beauvais Lamoureux points out that the boys behind the movement were invited to appear on TV shows, while very few women were heard on the subject.
« On va souvent donner le micro à des ho: “We often hand the mic to men. Of course, they have a right to an opinion, and I’m not questioning their credibility, but it might be interesting to have a female perspective on the question,” she says. She has no intention of criticizing the movement itself. “It’s a noble action, it’s great to see boys being allies of the feminist cause, wanting to be activists, being aware of their privileges and wanting to use them to help women emancipate themselves,” she stresses. What bothers her is the difference in treatment, reception and perception when women make demands.
« Les gens qui détiennent le pouvoir déc: “People who hold decision-making power will only be inclined to listen to these messages when young men are the ones carrying them. I find that sad,” she laments. After the school’s reaction, in which it said it was proud of the boys who took action, Alexandrine Beauvais Lamoureux and several Collège Jean-Eudes alumni mobilized to write an open letter, published in Le Devoir, and to speak out on social media.
« Nous avons seulement obtenu de la visi: “We only got media visibility thanks to opportunities we created ourselves,” she believes. Beauvais Lamoureux also made the decision to contact the school’s administration to talk about the issue, which led to the action plan she is now working on.
Thierry Lindor juge que Parle à tes boys: Thierry Lindor believes Parle à tes boys brings nothing new.
« Ce sont des choses qui ont été dites p: “These are things that have been said by women who are stronger, smarter, more resilient and more courageous than we are,” he says. Will Prosper agrees, adding that above all he doesn’t want to overshadow the women who have been carrying this movement for a long time.
« On s’assure de faire ce travail pour n: “We’re making sure we do this work so we don’t add to women’s labour, and to honour their work,” he sums up. According to Mr. Lindor, the four instigators, who each have their own areas of expertise, could have stuck to what they do best. They chose instead to use their platforms for the cause.
« On essaie de pousser cette conversatio: “We’re trying to push this conversation and help people understand its importance, while knowing that our role isn’t to replace women,” he explains. He would rather use his privileges to amplify their voices, for example by sharing resources developed by women, on their advice, and by inviting them to speak on his platform. “We’re at the beginning of a necessary discussion,” he says. “We want to do it by lifting up women’s voices.”
Si les événements tragiques incitent à p: While tragic events push people to act quickly, Marina Mathieu wants the work to be done more proactively in the future. “We can’t just talk about violence because we’re reacting to the deaths of women. What led to this situation?” she asks. The consultant names, for example, mental health, which she believes must be at the centre of the discussion.
La plupart du temps, cet aspect est abor: Most of the time, this aspect is addressed by women, who work in the background.
« Les femmes sont à la tête de ces initi: “Women are leading these initiatives; we can’t just react to the problems, because we live them.”
Pour plusieurs femmes, il est difficile: For many women, it is hard to trust the men who take part in the public debate. Marina Mathieu worries that the men who speak out are not necessarily aware of their own behaviours stemming from toxic masculinity. “They have to talk to themselves before they talk to each other,” she says.
« C’est important de voir comment la per: “It’s important to see how the person behaves in private. Behind closed doors, how do people act with women in general?” Kharoll-Ann Souffrant says in turn. This transparency is necessary. “I believe in redemption, in restorative justice, everyone makes mistakes and can learn.
Tout est dans la manière de faire. Avant: It’s all in how you go about it. Before talking about others, you have to take responsibility for your actions and your words, and apologize,” she concludes. Thierry Lindor and Will Prosper have begun a process of personal reflection, and a journey on this subject since the beginning, they tell us in an interview. They believe the four spokespeople are each doing individual work, notably by taking training.
« En deux semaines, j’ai appris plus que: “In two weeks, I learned more than in the last 30 years of my life, and I own that,” says Thierry Lindor. The process led him to revisit his past and to analyze all the relationships with women – romantic, friendly, professional and otherwise – that he may have had. For Will Prosper, this is part of the work. He reflects on the behaviours men sometimes have. “Are we going to be quicker to interrupt if it’s a woman?
Est-ce qu’on va vouloir dominer et étein: Are we going to want to dominate and shut down her voice? Am I really going to listen, or just repeat what she said and take her idea?” he asks. While conversations about toxic masculinity are new for many people, they are also new in many respects for the initiators of Parle à tes boys, who are not immune to questionable behaviour.
« Il ne faut pas penser qu’on est parfai: “We shouldn’t think we’re perfect. We’re constantly reflecting on how we can improve. That means going back and talking things through,” Will Prosper continues. His colleague agrees. “We know we’re clumsy. The fight is just beginning, we’re going to make more mistakes. We’re asking people to arm themselves with patience, not pity. We really want to change things.”
« Ce n’est pas hommes contre femmes. Ce: “It’s not men against women. It’s people against oppression coming together,” believes Thierry Lindor. He thinks the fact that four racialized men took this initiative says a lot. “For a Black man, it may be easier to understand the oppression women experience, because he also experiences oppression,” he suggests. Marina Mathieu doesn’t feel this unity.
« On travaille soi-même à la cause de to: “We work on everyone’s cause ourselves, without everyone being involved in the process,” she says of women who feel left behind. She wants to get people to question themselves more, especially about how they go about things. “It’s my right to ask, because people speak for me when they say they’re speaking on behalf of our communities.” Several Black women we spoke to told us about their experience with the “misogynoir” they face when they speak out – a term coined by researcher Moya Bailey to describe the distrust of and prejudice against Black women.
Un phénomène souvent internalisé, même d: It is a phenomenon that is often internalized, even within Black communities, we are told. “Violence isn’t only physical or psychological abuse. It’s the lack of recognition for the work and initiatives of Black women,” says Marina Mathieu. “What are we perpetuating today? How have you contributed to oppressing me or making me ‘invisible’?” she asks male allies.
Le danger d’effacement est malgré tout b: The danger of erasure is nonetheless very real. Kharoll-Ann Souffrant reminds us that it is often forgotten that the #MeToo movement was started by Tarana Burke. “She founded it precisely because no one protects Black women, and we often see the same thing,” she notes. One can also cite the Black Lives Matter movement, founded by three Black, queer women, or the fact that one of the first shelters in Canada was opened by a Black woman, Senator Anne Cools. “We have to protect all Black women, even those who challenge us, who have the courage to call out our contradictions,” she adds. Ms. Mathieu fears seeing the same power dynamics reproduced.
« On crée des organisations qui reprodui: “We create organizations that reproduce the same problematic hierarchical structures we denounce elsewhere,” she argues. It is also difficult to share space and act strategically in collaboration when Black people are given so little voice in the public sphere. “Unfortunately, that contributes to making the most vulnerable people in our communities ‘invisible.’”
« J’aimerais que des femmes noires autoc: “I’d like Black Indigenous women to tell us how we can do better,” says Thierry Lindor. “We slip up, but it’s not bad faith. It comes from a desire for change,” he continues. Will Prosper also hopes to build a common front. “I strongly believe in a diversity of tactics. I look a lot at allies – white people – to see how they dealt with the movement against racism. It’s an inspiration,” he tells us. But is it up to women to educate men about their behaviour?
Plusieurs femmes auxquelles nous avons p: Several women we spoke to believe that men must do their own introspection to dismantle their toxic masculinity before asking women to do that work for them.
